method: Sources were inspected first and pages written from what the passages state. No page was created before its evidence existed.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 5: Gamma Function
inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter title and DLMF release 1.2.7, dated 2026-06-15, confirmed on the chapter page before the sections were read.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
exactLocators: 5.5.3 reflection formula with its excluded points
5.11.1 Stirling expansion with its sector of validity

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The gamma function is fixed by a recurrence, and two further relations carry an argument across the half-plane and between scales.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 5.5.1 states Gamma(z+1) equals z times Gamma(z). 5.5.3 states Gamma(z) times Gamma(1-z) equals pi over sin(pi z), for z not zero and not a negative integer. 5.5.5 states the duplication formula, Gamma(2z) equals pi to the minus one half, times 2 to the power 2z-1, times Gamma(z) times Gamma(z+1/2), for 2z not zero and not a negative integer.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Large arguments are handled by an expansion that is asymptotic rather than convergent, so accuracy is bounded by the smallest term rather than by the number of terms taken.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 5.11.1 gives the Stirling series for the logarithm of Gamma(z) as z tends to infinity in the sector where the phase of z is at most pi minus delta. The relation is written with the asymptotic symbol, which the chapter identifies as a Poincare asymptotic expansion rather than a convergent series. 5.11.2 gives the corresponding expansion for the digamma function under the same sector condition.

inspected.establishes: The functional relations that define and compute the gamma function, each with the conditions the reference attaches to it.
inspected.boundary: States identities at their declared scope. It does not establish that any implementation attains a stated accuracy, and an asymptotic expansion carries no error bound from the term count alone.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 7: Error Function, Dawson Integral, and Fresnel Integrals
inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for Chapter 5.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The error function and its complement are defined as normalised integrals of the Gaussian kernel, and the two are related by a stated identity.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 7.2.1 defines erf z as two over the square root of pi, times the integral of exp of minus t squared from zero to z. 7.2.2 defines erfc z as the same normalised integral taken from z to infinity, and states in the same equation that erfc z equals one minus erf z.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The chapter defines the Dawson and Fresnel integrals alongside the error function, and records all of them as entire functions.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 7.2.5 defines the Dawson integral F(z) as exp of minus z squared times the integral of exp of t squared from zero to z. 7.2.7 and 7.2.8 define the Fresnel integrals C(z) and S(z) as the integrals of cosine and sine of pi t squared over two. The chapter records these as entire functions of the complex variable.

inspected.establishes: Integral definitions for the error function, its complement, the Dawson integral and the Fresnel integrals, with the identity relating erf and erfc.
inspected.boundary: Defines the functions and their relations. It does not establish the accuracy of any implementation, and no statistical interpretation follows from a definition.

inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 10: Bessel Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for Chapters 5 and 7.
exactLocators: 10.2.1 the differential equation and its singularity structure

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The equation has a stated singularity structure, and its first-kind solution is a series whose coefficients are gamma values.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 10.2.1 states the equation as z squared w double prime plus z w prime plus the quantity z squared minus nu squared times w equals zero, and records that it has a regular singularity at z equals zero with indices plus and minus nu and an irregular singularity of rank one at infinity. 10.2.2 gives the first-kind solution as a power series in which the k-th coefficient divides by the gamma function at nu plus k plus one, and notes it is analytic except for a branch point at the origin when nu is not an integer.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The second solution is constructed from the first and degenerates at integer order, and choosing a pair is a question of region rather than of independence alone.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 10.2.3 builds the second-kind solution from first-kind solutions of order plus and minus nu, divided by sine of nu pi. 10.2.4 supplies the limiting form at integer order where that construction degenerates. The chapter records that the second-kind solution has a branch point at the origin whether or not nu is an integer, with a cut along the negative reals, and Table 10.2.1 tabulates which pairs are numerically satisfactory in which region.

inspected.establishes: The Bessel equation, its singularity structure, both standard solutions, and which pairs are numerically satisfactory by region.
inspected.boundary: States the solutions and their analytic structure. It does not select a pair for a given computation, and makes no accuracy claim about any implementation.

inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 24: Bernoulli and Euler Polynomials
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for Chapters 5, 7 and 10.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The Bernoulli numbers and polynomials are defined by generating functions that converge only inside a stated disk.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 24.2.1 defines the Bernoulli numbers by t over the quantity e to the t minus one, expanded as a sum of B sub n times t to the n over n factorial, stated to converge for the modulus of t less than two pi. 24.2.3 gives the polynomials from the same expression multiplied by e to the x t in the same disk, and 24.2.4 records that B sub n equals B sub n of zero.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Odd-indexed coefficients vanish apart from one exception, and the Euler generating function converges in a strictly smaller disk than the Bernoulli one.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 24.2.2 states that odd-indexed Bernoulli numbers vanish apart from the first, and that the even ones alternate in sign with minus one to the n plus one times B sub two n positive for n at least one. 24.2.6 defines the Euler numbers by two e to the t over the quantity e to the two t plus one, converging only for the modulus of t less than pi over two, and 24.2.7 states that odd-indexed Euler numbers vanish.

inspected.crossPageNote: The vanishing rule at 24.2.2 explains a feature of the gamma page: the Stirling expansion at 5.11.1 is indexed by even numbers because the odd Bernoulli coefficients are zero. Both halves of that observation are inspected.
inspected.establishes: Generating-function definitions with their convergence radii, and the vanishing and sign rules for odd and even indices.
inspected.boundary: Defines the coefficients inside stated disks. It makes no claim about the numerical stability of any recurrence used to generate them.

inspected.title: Asteroseismology Using The Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey
inspected.identifier: science.nasa.gov Roman Space Telescope survey description
inspected.identityBasis: Publisher and page title confirmed on retrieval.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government agency publication, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
exactLocators: Properties measured for tens of thousands of stars

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The observable is a long, regularly sampled photometric series, from which an oscillation frequency pattern is characterised.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: NASA states that the approach relies on precise, regularly sampled, long-duration photometric observations to characterise the oscillation frequency pattern of evolved red giants, which it describes as high-amplitude non-radial oscillators.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Masses, radii and ages are inferred only in combination with separately measured metallicity and temperature, and saturation remains an open constraint.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: NASA states that masses, radii and ages have been measured for tens of thousands of stars using asteroseismic data combined with stellar metallicity and effective temperature. It also states that saturation will be important for red clump stars in the Galactic bulge, and describes an improved asteroseismic detection model including the effect of saturation as work to be developed.

inspected.notCovered: The page does not explain why the oscillations occur, and gives no frequencies, amplitudes or precision figures. The page built on it therefore records the driving mechanism as unestablished and makes no numerical accuracy claim.
inspected.establishes: The asteroseismic observable, the properties inferred from it in combination with other measurements, and the saturation constraint the survey still faces.
inspected.boundary: A mission survey description. It establishes the method's inputs and outputs, not the physics behind them or any precision figure.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 2: Asymptotic Approximations

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Asymptotic equality and the order symbols are defined by the behaviour of a ratio in a stated limit, so each is meaningless without that limit.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 2.1.1 defines f asymptotic to phi as the ratio of the two tending to one as x tends to c within a point set X. 2.1.2 defines f equals little-o of phi as the ratio tending to zero in the same limit, and 2.1.3 defines f equals big-O of phi as the modulus of the ratio being bounded. Each definition is stated relative to the limit point c and the point set X.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: A Poincare expansion is a condition on every truncation, and it does not determine the function it describes.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 2.1.13 requires that for each positive integer n the function equals the sum of the first n terms plus a remainder of order x to the minus n, and 2.1.14 writes the resulting expansion with the tilde. The chapter states that a series converging for all sufficiently large modulus is automatically the asymptotic expansion of its sum, and gives zero, e to the minus z, and e to the minus z cosine z as functions all possessing the null asymptotic expansion in suitable sectors.

inspected.crossPageNote: Generalises the limitation recorded on the gamma page: Stirling at 5.11.1 is one instance of a Poincare expansion as defined at 2.1.13, which is why adding terms eventually makes it worse.
inspected.establishes: What an asymptotic statement means, and that an expansion is shared by more than one function.
inspected.boundary: Defines the notation and the expansion. It makes no accuracy claim at any particular argument.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 18: Orthogonal Polynomials
exactLocators: 18.2.1 and 18.2.1_5 continuous orthogonality and the weight conditions

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Orthogonality is defined against a declared weight or measure that must itself satisfy stated conditions.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 18.2.1 states that distinct members of the family integrate to zero against each other over an open interval with weight w. 18.2.1_5 requires w to be non-negative, to have positive total integral, and to have all moments finite. 18.2.2 and 18.2.3 give the discrete analogues over infinite and finite point sets, and 18.2.4_5 gives the general form against a Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Two standard three-term recurrences carry the family, and strict positivity conditions give the converse through Favard theorem.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 18.2.8 gives the recurrence in the form p n plus one equals the quantity A n x plus B n times p n, minus C n times p n minus one, for n at least zero. 18.2.10 gives the second form, x times p n equals a n p n plus one plus b n p n plus c n p n minus one. Both are stated with strict positivity conditions at 18.2.9_5 and 18.2.11_2 which ensure orthogonality by Favard theorem.

inspected.establishes: Orthogonality conditions across the continuous, discrete and measure-theoretic settings, and the recurrences with the positivity that makes the converse hold.
inspected.boundary: States conditions and recurrences. It does not establish numerical stability, and orthogonality is relative to a declared weight.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 25: Zeta and Related Functions
exactLocators: 25.2.4 and 25.2.5 the Laurent expansion and Stieltjes constants

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Two representations agree in one half-plane and define the function nowhere else.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 25.2.1 states that when the real part of s exceeds one, zeta of s is the sum over n of one over n to the s. 25.2.11 states the Euler product, zeta of s equals the product over primes p of one minus p to the minus s, all inverted, under the same condition that the real part of s exceeds one.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: Values elsewhere come from continuation, and the continued function has exactly one singularity.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: The chapter states that elsewhere zeta is defined by analytic continuation, and that it is a meromorphic function whose only singularity in the complex plane is a simple pole at s equals one with residue one. 25.2.4 gives the Laurent expansion about that pole as one over s minus one plus a series whose coefficients are the Stieltjes constants, and 25.2.5 defines those constants as limits of a difference between a partial sum and a logarithmic term.

inspected.notCovered: The relation between zeta at even integers and the Bernoulli numbers was asked for and not returned by this retrieval, so no such claim is made on the page despite the adjacent Bernoulli page existing.
inspected.establishes: The two representations with their shared half-plane, the analytic continuation, and the single pole with its local expansion.
inspected.boundary: States representations and analytic structure. It settles nothing about the zeros.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 15: Hypergeometric Function
exactLocators: 15.2.1 the Gauss series with its branch and cut

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The series is defined on the unit disk with a declared branch, is undefined for a family of parameter values, and a regularized form exists to remove that exception.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 15.2.1 defines F of a, b; c; z as a series in Pochhammer symbols on the disk where the modulus of z is less than one, and by analytic continuation elsewhere, with the principal branch taken where the phase of one minus z is at most pi and a cut from one to positive infinity along the real axis. The chapter states that in general F does not exist when c is zero or a negative integer. 15.2.2 gives the regularized form, which divides by a gamma function and is stated to be valid for all values of c and analytic at those exceptional points.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The series terminates for one family of parameters, and its behaviour on the boundary circle splits into three regimes by a single condition.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 15.2.4 states that when the upper parameter a equals minus m for a non-negative integer m, and c is not zero or a negative integer, the function is a polynomial with a finite sum representation. On the circle where the modulus of z equals one, the chapter states that the series converges absolutely when the real part of c minus a minus b exceeds zero, converges conditionally when that real part lies between minus one and zero excluding the point z equals one, and diverges when it is at or below minus one.

inspected.establishes: The Gauss series with its disk, branch and exceptional parameters, the regularized form, the termination condition, and the three boundary regimes.
inspected.boundary: A definition with a declared branch. It does not establish the accuracy of any numerical continuation outside the disk.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 8: Incomplete Gamma and Related Functions
inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for the earlier chapters.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The gamma integral splits at a point into two halves whose sum is the complete function.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 8.2.1 defines the lower incomplete gamma as the integral of t to the a minus one times e to the minus t from zero to z, for real part of a greater than zero. 8.2.2 defines the upper form as the same integrand from z to infinity. 8.2.3 states that the lower plus the upper equals the complete gamma at a, for a not equal to zero or a negative integer.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The normalized pair sums to one exactly, and the two halves differ in their analytic structure in the parameter.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 8.2.4 defines P of a, z as the lower form divided by the complete gamma and Q of a, z as the upper form divided by the same, and 8.2.5 states that P plus Q equals one. The chapter records that the upper incomplete gamma is entire in a when z is non-zero, while the lower is meromorphic with simple poles at a equal to the non-positive integers.

inspected.crossPageNote: The exact identity at 8.2.5 is the same device as 7.2.2 on the error-function page: a complementary form exists so the small member can be computed directly rather than by subtracting the large one from one. Both halves of that observation are inspected.
inspected.establishes: The two integral halves, the identity binding them to the complete gamma, the normalized pair, and their differing analytic structure.
inspected.boundary: Defines the functions and their relation. It makes no accuracy claim for any evaluation method.

inspected.title: Very Long Baseline Interferometry
inspected.identityBasis: Publisher and page title confirmed on retrieval.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government agency publication, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.

claimByClaimSupport.locator: What VLBI measures; the stated precisions
claimByClaimSupport.claim: The observable is an arrival-time difference between two antennas, and the stated precisions carry from time to position to sky angle.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: NASA states that VLBI measures the time difference between the arrival at two Earth-based antennas of a radio wavefront emitted by a distant quasar, that the time difference measurements are precise to a few picoseconds, and that this determines the relative positions of the antennas to a few millimetres and the quasar positions to fractions of a milliarcsecond.

claimByClaimSupport.locator: What the technique determines; the inertial assumption
claimByClaimSupport.claim: Three products come out together, and the inertial anchor is an assumption with a stated reason rather than a given.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: NASA states that VLBI determines the terrestrial reference frame of antenna locations on the Earth, the celestial reference frame of quasar positions on the sky, and the orientation of the Earth in space, and that it is unique in making rapid accurate measurements of the orientation of one frame with respect to the other. It states that extragalactic objects form a true inertial reference frame because they are at such great distances that their motions across the sky are undetectable.

inspected.notCovered: The page does not derive the relation between baseline length and angular resolution, so the page built on it states no resolution formula.
inspected.establishes: The VLBI observable, its stated precisions, the three products of the technique, and the reason given for treating extragalactic sources as inertial.
inspected.boundary: An agency technique description. The precisions are stated capabilities rather than results for a particular observation.

inspected.title: DLMF Chapter 19: Elliptic Integrals
inspected.venue: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions
inspected.identityBasis: Chapter and section identified on retrieval against the same DLMF release confirmed for the earlier chapters.
inspected.rightsBasis: United States government reference work, publicly readable. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.
exactLocators: 19.2.7 third kind and its principal value

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The first two kinds are defined with shared domain conditions, and the complete forms are those integrals at quarter period.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 19.2.4 defines F of phi and k as the integral from zero to phi of d theta over the square root of one minus k squared sine squared theta. 19.2.5 defines E of phi and k with that square root in the numerator. Both require one minus sine squared phi and one minus k squared sine squared phi to lie outside the cut along the non-positive reals, with at most one of them equal to zero. 19.2.8 defines K of k, E of k and Pi of alpha squared and k as those integrals evaluated at phi equal to pi over two.

claimByClaimSupport.claim: The third kind carries an extra condition and needs a principal value where that condition fails inside the range.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: 19.2.7 defines Pi of phi, alpha squared and k with an additional factor of one minus alpha squared sine squared theta in the denominator, requiring one minus alpha squared sine squared phi to be non-zero, and states that the Cauchy principal value applies if that expression vanishes at an interior point of integration. The principal branch is declared where the phase of one minus k squared is at most pi, with branch cuts on the reals outside minus one to one.

inspected.establishes: The three Legendre kinds with their domain conditions, the principal-value case, and the complete forms.
inspected.boundary: Defines the integrals and where they fail. It makes no accuracy claim about any evaluation scheme.

inspected.title: Calendars and their History
inspected.venue: L. E. Doggett, University Science Books, hosted by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center
inspected.identityBasis: Author, publisher and title confirmed on retrieval. Recorded as Doggett's chapter hosted by NASA rather than as a NASA publication, because the two are different authorities.
inspected.rightsBasis: Publicly readable on a United States government host. Retrieved without circumventing any access control.

claimByClaimSupport.locator: The stated mean periods and the lunar year
claimByClaimSupport.claim: Two measured periods are incommensurable, and twelve lunar months fall short of the tropical year by a computable amount.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: Doggett gives the tropical year as 365.2421896698 days and the mean synodic month as 29.5305888531 days, and states the lunar year of twelve synodic months as 354.36707 days. Multiplying the stated synodic month by twelve reproduces that figure exactly, and subtracting it from the stated tropical year gives a shortfall of about 10.875 days.

claimByClaimSupport.locator: The three families, the Metonic relation and the Gregorian cycle
claimByClaimSupport.claim: Three families of scheme answer the mismatch differently, each carrying a residual.
claimByClaimSupport.supportingPassage: Doggett describes a solar calendar as maintaining synchrony with the tropical year by intercalating days, naming the Gregorian with its 400-year cycle of 146,097 days averaging 365.2425 days. A lunar calendar follows the phase cycle without regard for the tropical year, named as the Islamic calendar. A lunisolar calendar intercalates a whole month every few years using the Metonic relation that 235 lunations occur in nineteen years, 6939.688 days, named as the Hebrew and Chinese calendars.

inspected.arithmeticCheck: Both derived figures reproduce the source exactly: twelve synodic months give 354.36707 days as stated, and 235 synodic months give 6939.6884 days against the stated 6939.688. One figure does not reconcile: the Gregorian average of 365.2425 exceeds the stated tropical year by 0.00031 days per year, which is one day in about 3200 years, while Doggett states about one day in 2500. The page reports the derived figure and records the source's, and attributes the gap to which definition of the tropical year is used rather than claiming to resolve it.
inspected.frameNote: Recorded as secondary historical scholarship, not as formal mathematics and not as religious evidence. It establishes calendar arithmetic and which communities use which family; it establishes nothing about observance, which may be set by sighting rather than computation.
inspected.establishes: The three calendar families, the mean periods behind them, and the reconciliation schemes each uses with their residuals.
inspected.boundary: Calendar arithmetic and history. It determines no observance and predicts no individual month.

heldBack.notAttachedReason: Inspected at section level and ready to attach, but held back. The route it supports, /knowledge/astronomy/exoplanet-detection-and-confirmation, is one of the twenty records in the Phase 4 pilot, whose manifest carries a frozen sha256. That manifest is recomputed from live data rather than stored, so adding any source to a pilot record moves the digest: this source took the blocker count from 87 to 89. Every existing astronomy source carries the same two blockers, a missing publication date and a missing locator, so the source is no worse than its neighbours; the coupling is the issue. Updating a frozen release-governance digest to accommodate a content addition is a decision for a person, not a side effect of adding a page.
